entry.title: Fifth Circuit Affirms Dismissal of Jackson Water Contamination Lawsuit
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | motherjones.com | source | hacker news

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal of a lawsuit brought by Jackson, Mississippi residents alleging that the city's failure to prevent lead-contaminated water exposure violated their constitutional rights. Judge Kurt Engelhardt ruled that the U.S. Constitution does not grant a right to truthful information from officials or a right to clean water during a public health crisis.

The ruling follows years of infrastructure neglect in the majority-Black, high-poverty city, where lead levels have been a concern since at least 2015. While several U.S. states and various international governments have enshrined the right to clean water in their constitutions, the federal ruling limits the scope of such constitutional claims. The decision coincides with recent EPA proposals to weaken Clean Water Act protections.

entry.content:

A United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report warns that Earth is expected to exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius warming threshold established by the Paris Agreement within the next few years. The report outlines an "overshoot" strategy, suggesting that the world must first limit the peak temperature and then use carbon removal and fossil fuel phase-outs to return to safer levels to minimize long-term damage.

Current global policies project temperatures to reach 2.6°C above pre-industrial levels by 2100, though ambitious goals could cap warming at 1.8°C by mid-century. The transition period of overshoot is expected to last decades, causing increased extreme weather, rising sea levels, and food shortages. Experts emphasize that managing this period requires significant investment in climate adaptation and novel carbon dioxide removal technologies.

entry.title: Binghamton University Study Finds Aging Brains Blend Memories Through Category-Level Misbinding
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | studyfinds.com | source | hacker news

Aging brains may undergo "category-level misbinding," a process where the brain retrieves information too broadly and confuses different categories of items, such as objects and scenes, instead of simply forgetting them. Using MRI scans, researchers found that hippocampal activity in older adults lacks the precise overlap between learning and recall patterns seen in younger adults, instead predicting these specific types of errors.

This phenomenon suggests that aging affects the precision of memory reactivation rather than just the strength of the memory trace. The study noted that this shift is not fully explained by hippocampal shrinkage or declines in attention, indicating a potential fundamental change in the brain's ability to keep similar episodic memories distinct.
